title: How to check if a charity is legitimate
summary: How to check if a charity is legit: confirm it is registered, that its record matches the appeal and that its people are real. Sixtyfour researches who runs it.
body_markdown:
Look it up by its exact legal name or registration number in the official register, such as the IRS's Tax Exempt Organization Search in the US, the Charity Commission's register in England and Wales or the Canada Revenue Agency's List of charities, and check that the record matches the name, address and people in the appeal. Then confirm that the appeal comes from that charity by contacting it through its own website or filings, and be wary of pressure to give at once or of requests to pay by gift card, wire transfer, payment app or cryptocurrency.


Search the IRS's Tax Exempt Organization Search by the charity's EIN or its legal name. It shows the organisation's tax-exempt status and filings: its Pub. 78 entry, its Form 990 series returns or Form 990-N notices, its determination letters, and whether it appears on the automatic revocation list. Organisations are listed under the legal name or a "doing business as" name the IRS has on file, so a campaign name may return nothing.


In England and Wales, search the Charity Commission's register of charities by name or number; each record shows the charity's trustees, finances and contact details and whether its accounts and annual returns arrived on time. Scotland and Northern Ireland keep separate registers. In Canada, search the Canada Revenue Agency's List of charities, which shows whether a charity is "registered, revoked, annulled, penalized, or suspended", with the public parts of the T3010 returns it filed for its last five fiscal periods.


Between them, the FTC and the Canada Revenue Agency list pressure to give right away, thanks for a pledge you do not remember making, a name that sounds like a well-known charity, and requests to pay in cash, by gift card, by wiring money, through a payment app or in cryptocurrency. Other signs are a caller ID or sender that only looks right, a free email address, emotional claims with few details about how the money will be used, and photos or stories copied from somewhere else.


Check how long the organisation has existed, from its registration, its first filing and its first mention in sources it does not control, and when its website's domain was created. Run its photos through a reverse image search, because the FTC warns that scammers often use stolen photos and copy other people's stories. The FTC's advice after a disaster is to give to charities you know and trust, with a proven track record in dealing with disasters.


Yes. Sixtyfour is a research agent that takes a charity's name and website and the people its appeal names, researches sources across the web, and returns the answers you ask for, such as who leads the charity, when it first appears outside its own pages and whether an appeal connects to it, each with the page it was read on and, when you ask, a confidence score for each field. Anything it could not establish comes back empty for a person on your team to decide.


Contact your bank, card issuer or payment app at once and ask it to reverse the payment, and keep the appeal, the payment details and every message. In the US, report it to the FTC and to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center. In the UK, the government's Donate with Confidence campaign says to report a fake appeal to Report Fraud, and in Canada the Canada Revenue Agency points to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre for organisations that pose as charities without being registered.
